nameStory: The Well-ribbed Dove Snail gets its name from the prominent raised ridges (ribs) that spiral around its shell, giving it a distinctly textured appearance. The "dove" part comes from the family name - these small, compact snails were thought to resemble the gentle, rounded shape of a dove when viewed from certain angles.
description: The Well-ribbed Dove Snail is a tiny marine snail that lives along New England's rocky shores and tide pools. These small gastropods (the scientific term for snails and slugs) have distinctive spiral shells marked with raised ridges that you can actually feel with your fingertip. They're typically less than half an inch long, making them easy to overlook among the rocks and seaweed. Like other sea snails, they glide along on a muscular foot, grazing on algae and organic matter.

idTips.label: Ribbed Shell Texture
idTips.description: The shell feels bumpy to the touch due to distinct raised ribs that spiral around from top to bottom - run your finger along it and you'll feel the regular ridges

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Typically smaller than your pinky nail, usually measuring less than half an inch from tip to opening

idTips.label: Spiral Shell Shape
idTips.description: Classic cone-shaped spiral shell that tapers to a pointed tip, wider at the opening where the snail emerges

idTips.label: Brown to Gray Coloring
idTips.description: Shell ranges from light brown to grayish-white, often with darker bands or mottling that helps it blend with rocky surfaces

idTips.label: Thick Shell Walls
idTips.description: The shell feels solid and sturdy for its size - not paper-thin like some other small marine snails

habitat: Look for Well-ribbed Dove Snails in rocky intertidal zones along New England's coast, especially in tide pools and on wave-splashed rocks. They prefer areas with moderate wave action where they can graze on algae growing on rock surfaces. You'll often find them tucked into crevices or under ledges during low tide, particularly in areas with coralline algae and other small marine organisms.

seasonality.spring: Active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found grazing on early algae growth on rocks. Look for them during low tides on sunny days when they're most active.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot moving around tide pools and rocky surfaces. This is the best time to observe their feeding behavior and see them fully extended from their shells.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek more sheltered locations. Often found deeper in rock crevices as water temperatures start to cool.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find, typically hiding in protected spots under rocks or in deep crevices. Empty shells may wash up on beaches after winter storms.

funFact: Despite being tiny, Well-ribbed Dove Snails are surprisingly tough - they can actually sense approaching waves and clamp down tightly to rocks, withstanding forces that would knock much larger creatures loose from their perch!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Greedy Dove Snail, but the Well-ribbed has much more pronounced spiral ridges that you can clearly feel with your finger, while the Greedy Dove Snail has a smoother shell surface. Memory trick: "Well-ribbed" means you can feel the ribs well!
contextualKnowledge: The name "dove snail" might seem odd for a marine creature, but it refers to the family's typically small, compact, rounded shells that early naturalists thought resembled a dove's body. Don't confuse these marine snails with land snails - they need saltwater to survive and will quickly die if removed from their tidal environment.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Greedy Dove Snail, the Well-ribbed Dove Snail has much more prominent spiral ribs that create a noticeably bumpy texture you can feel with your fingertip. The Greedy Dove Snail has a relatively smooth shell surface with only faint growth lines. Both are similar in size and general shape, but the ribbing is the key difference between these two New England species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Greedy Dove Snail differs from its close relative, the Well-ribbed Dove Snail, primarily in shell sculpture - the Well-ribbed species has much more prominent spiral ridges that you can easily feel with your finger, while the Greedy Dove Snail's shell surface is relatively smooth.
